descripcion_es: Use of commas; which referring to a whole clause; preposition + whom/which.
resumen: Non-defining relative clauses add extra information about something already identified and go between commas. In them you cannot use that or leave out the pronoun.

explicacion.texto: Defining (no commas): it identifies who or what we are talking about. The students who failed must repeat the exam (only the ones who failed). Non-defining (with commas): it adds a piece of information. The students, who were tired, went home (all the students).

filas: My aunt, who lives in Bilbao, is a judge.
Mr Patel, whom I met in Delhi, sent me a book.
things, animals or the whole previous clause
The museum, which opened in 1900, is free.
Ana, whose husband is a pilot, travels a lot.
Toledo, where I grew up, is beautiful.

items: Never that in a non-defining clause: My car, which is red… (not “, that is red”).
The pronoun cannot be left out, even when it is the object.
Which can refer to the whole previous clause: He passed the exam, which surprised everyone (Spanish “lo cual / lo que”).
Preposition + whom/which (formal): The director, to whom I wrote, never replied. Informal: The director, who I wrote to, never replied.
Quantifier + of whom / of which: I have three brothers, two of whom live abroad.

ejemplos.frase: Lisbon, which is built on seven hills, is great for walking.
ejemplos.traduccion: Lisboa, que está construida sobre siete colinas, es ideal para pasear.

ejemplos.frase: The train was cancelled, which meant we had to take a taxi.
ejemplos.traduccion: Cancelaron el tren, lo que significó que tuvimos que coger un taxi.

ejemplos.frase: My neighbour, whose dog barks all night, has finally moved.
ejemplos.traduccion: Mi vecino, cuyo perro ladra toda la noche, por fin se ha mudado.

ejemplos.frase: The minister, with whom I had a brief conversation, seemed optimistic.
ejemplos.traduccion: El ministro, con quien tuve una breve conversación, parecía optimista.

ejemplos.frase: She bought twenty books, most of which she has never read.
ejemplos.traduccion: Compró veinte libros, la mayoría de los cuales no ha leído nunca.

ejemplos.frase: In 1992, when the Olympics took place, the city changed completely.
ejemplos.traduccion: En 1992, cuando se celebraron los Juegos Olímpicos, la ciudad cambió por completo.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: He lost his keys, what was annoying.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: He lost his keys, which was annoying.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Spanish “lo que” referring to the previous clause is which, not what.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: My brother, that is a doctor, lives in Leeds.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: My brother, who is a doctor, lives in Leeds.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: That is not used in non-defining relative clauses.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I have two sisters, both of them are teachers.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I have two sisters, both of whom are teachers.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: To join the clauses you need the relative pronoun: of whom / of which.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the correct relative pronoun.
ejercicios.frase: Our teacher, ___ wife is Italian, speaks four languages.
ejercicios.explicacion: The whose row of the pronoun table applies: whose expresses possession, like Spanish “cuyo”. The clue is that a noun, wife, comes straight after the gap and belongs to the antecedent (the teacher's wife). Whose is followed by the possessed noun with no article: “whose wife”. No other relative form can go before a noun with that possessive meaning.
ejercicios.traduccion: Nuestro profesor, cuya mujer es italiana, habla cuatro idiomas.

errores_previstos.respuesta: who
errores_previstos.explicacion: Who is a subject or object, it does not show possession; “who wife” makes no sense. You need whose, equivalent to Spanish “cuya”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: who's
errores_previstos.explicacion: Who's is the contraction of who is or who has and sounds the same as whose, but “who is wife” makes no sense. The possessive is spelt whose.

errores_previstos.respuesta: that
errores_previstos.explicacion: That is never used in a non-defining relative clause (the clause is between commas) and, besides, it does not express possession.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the correct relative pronoun.
ejercicios.frase: She didn't answer my messages, ___ made me worried.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule from Rules and key points applies: which can refer to the whole previous clause, meaning “and this” (Spanish “lo cual” or “lo que”). The clue is that what worried me is not the messages but the whole fact that she did not answer. That is why the relative pronoun goes after the comma and picks up the whole idea: “, which made me worried”. Neither what nor that can do this job.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Which refers to the whole previous clause.
ejercicios.traduccion: No contestó a mis mensajes, lo cual me preocupó.

errores_previstos.respuesta: what
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is a calque of Spanish “lo que”. What has no antecedent and cannot refer back to a previous clause; which is used for that.

errores_previstos.respuesta: that
errores_previstos.explicacion: That is never used after a comma in a non-defining relative clause, and it cannot refer to a whole clause either.

errores_previstos.respuesta: it
errores_previstos.explicacion: It would turn the sentence into two clauses joined only by a comma (comma splice), which is incorrect in written English; you need the relative pronoun which.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the correct relative pronoun (formal register).
ejercicios.frase: The candidates, most of ___ had no experience, were all rejected.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule quantifier + of whom / of which from Rules and key points applies. The clue is the structure “most of ___” inside a parenthetical clause between commas, referring to people (the candidates). After a preposition, whom, the object form, is used for people: “most of whom”. In formal, written register it is the only correct option.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: After most of with people, use whom.
ejercicios.traduccion: Los candidatos, la mayoría de los cuales no tenía experiencia, fueron rechazados todos.

errores_previstos.respuesta: who
errores_previstos.explicacion: After a preposition (of) you do not use who but the object form whom: “most of whom”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: them
errores_previstos.explicacion: “Most of them” joins two clauses with no linking word; it is the typical Spanish speaker's mistake. To make it a relative clause you need the relative pronoun whom.

errores_previstos.respuesta: which
errores_previstos.explicacion: Which is used for things; the candidates are people, so whom is required.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the correct relative word.
ejercicios.frase: Seville, ___ my parents met, is my favourite city.
ejercicios.explicacion: The where / when row of the table applies: where introduces a relative clause of place and is equivalent to “in which”. The clue is that the antecedent is a place (Seville) and that the relative clause lacks an adverbial of place: my parents met there. Notice that the relative clause already has a subject (my parents) and a verb (met), so you do not need a subject pronoun such as which.
ejercicios.traduccion: Sevilla, donde se conocieron mis padres, es mi ciudad favorita.

errores_previstos.respuesta: which
errores_previstos.explicacion: Which would only work with a preposition (“in which my parents met”); on its own, it would leave the relative clause without the adverbial of place.

errores_previstos.respuesta: that
errores_previstos.explicacion: That never goes in a non-defining clause between commas and, besides, it does not express place.

errores_previstos.respuesta: in where
errores_previstos.explicacion: Where already includes the idea of “in”; adding in is redundant. Use either where or in which.

ejercicios.frase: The Prado, ___ attracts millions of visitors, is in Madrid.
ejercicios.explicacion: The first rule from Rules and key points applies: never that in a non-defining clause. The clues are the commas and the antecedent, the Prado, a unique place already identified: the clause between commas only adds a piece of information. As the antecedent is a thing and the relative pronoun is the subject of attracts, the correct form is which.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Non-defining clause referring to a thing: which, never that.
ejercicios.traduccion: El Prado, que atrae a millones de visitantes, está en Madrid.

por_opcion.which: Correct: a relative pronoun for things, allowed in non-defining clauses, which works here as the subject of attracts.
por_opcion.that: Incorrect: that works in defining clauses, but never after a comma in a non-defining clause.
por_opcion.what: Incorrect: what means “the thing that” and has no antecedent; here the antecedent is The Prado.
por_opcion.who: Incorrect: who is for people and the Prado is a museum.

ejercicios.frase: The hotel, in ___ we stayed for a week, was right on the beach.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule preposition + whom/which in formal register applies. The clues are the preposition in before the gap and the antecedent, the hotel, which is a thing. After a preposition, only which is possible for things: “in which we stayed”. That can never go after a preposition, and whom or who are for people.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Thing after a preposition: which (that never goes after a preposition).
ejercicios.traduccion: El hotel, en el que nos alojamos una semana, estaba justo en la playa.

por_opcion.whom: Incorrect: whom does go after a preposition, but only for people, and a hotel is a thing.
por_opcion.which: Correct: a thing after a preposition, “in which” (Spanish “en el que, en el cual”).
por_opcion.who: Incorrect: it is for people and, besides, it does not go after a preposition in formal register.
por_opcion.that: Incorrect on two counts: it goes neither after a preposition nor in non-defining clauses.

ejercicios.frase: He kept interrupting, ___ was very rude.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule of which referring to the whole previous clause applies, meaning “and this” (Spanish “lo cual”). The clue is that what is rude is not a person or an object but the fact of interrupting again and again. To pick up that whole idea after the comma, use which. It is a case where Spanish “lo que” tempts you to write what.
ejercicios.traduccion: No paraba de interrumpir, lo cual fue muy maleducado.

por_opcion.which: Correct: it refers back to the whole previous clause (Spanish “lo cual”).
por_opcion.what: Incorrect: a calque of Spanish “lo que”; what cannot refer to something already said.
por_opcion.that: Incorrect: it is not used after a comma in a non-defining clause and cannot refer to a whole clause.

ejercicios.frase: My best friend, that lives in Paris, is coming to visit.
respuestas: My best friend, who lives in Paris, is coming to visit.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule “never that in a non-defining clause” applies. The clue is the commas: “my best friend” is already identified (there is only one) and the clause between commas adds a piece of information. As the antecedent is a person and the relative pronoun is the subject of lives, the correct form is who: “My best friend, who lives in Paris, is coming to visit”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: That is not used in non-defining clauses; for people, use who.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mi mejor amigo, que vive en París, viene de visita.

errores_previstos.respuesta: My best friend, that lives in Paris, is coming to visit.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: that cannot go in a non-defining relative clause between commas.

errores_previstos.respuesta: My best friend, which lives in Paris, is coming to visit.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Which is for things; for a person, use who.

errores_previstos.respuesta: My best friend that lives in Paris is coming to visit.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Removing the commas turns it into a defining clause and suggests that you have several “best friends”; the real mistake is that, which must be changed to who while keeping the commas.

ejercicios.frase: The flight was delayed, what meant we missed our connection.
respuestas: The flight was delayed, which meant we missed our connection.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule of which referring to the whole previous clause applies. What caused us to miss the connection is not the flight itself but the fact that it was delayed, so you must refer back to the whole clause. The mistake is using what, a calque of Spanish “lo que”; the correct form is “, which meant we missed our connection”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Which, not what, to refer to the previous clause.
ejercicios.traduccion: El vuelo se retrasó, lo que hizo que perdiéramos la conexión.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The flight was delayed, what meant we missed our connection.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: what cannot refer back to a previous clause; you need which.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The flight was delayed, that meant we missed our connection.
errores_previstos.explicacion: That is not used in non-defining relative clauses after a comma; nor can it refer to the whole clause.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The flight was delayed, it meant we missed our connection.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Joining two independent clauses with just a comma is incorrect in English (comma splice); you need the relative pronoun which.

ejercicios.frase: I interviewed ten people, three of them had been unemployed for years.
respuestas: I interviewed ten people, three of whom had been unemployed for years.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule quantifier + of whom / of which applies. The original sentence joins two clauses with a simple comma using “three of them”, a calque of spoken Spanish. To make the second part a relative clause, you must replace the personal pronoun with the object relative pronoun for people: “three of whom”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: You need the relative pronoun: three of whom.
ejercicios.traduccion: Entrevisté a diez personas, tres de las cuales llevaban años en paro.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I interviewed ten people, three of them had been unemployed for years.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: two clauses joined only by a comma; you need the relative pronoun whom.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I interviewed ten people, three of who had been unemployed for years.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After the preposition of, use the object form whom, not who.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I interviewed ten people, three of which had been unemployed for years.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Which is for things; for people the quantifier goes with of whom.

ejercicios.enunciado: Join the two sentences with a non-defining relative clause (use who).
ejercicios.frase: Marie Curie won two Nobel prizes. She was born in Warsaw.
respuestas: Marie Curie, who was born in Warsaw, won two Nobel prizes.
Marie Curie, who won two Nobel prizes, was born in Warsaw.
ejercicios.explicacion: The central idea of the card applies: a non-defining relative clause adds a piece of information about an antecedent that is already identified and goes between commas, right after it. Marie Curie is a proper noun, so any additional information is non-defining. Replace the pronoun she with who and place the clause after the name. Both solutions are valid because either piece of information can be the main one and the other the added clause.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The extra information goes between commas after the name.
ejercicios.traduccion: Marie Curie, que nació en Varsovia, ganó dos premios Nobel. (También: Marie Curie, que ganó dos premios Nobel, nació en Varsovia.)

errores_previstos.respuesta: Marie Curie, which was born in Warsaw, won two Nobel prizes.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Which is for things; for a person like Marie Curie, use who.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Marie Curie, that was born in Warsaw, won two Nobel prizes.
errores_previstos.explicacion: That is not used in non-defining relative clauses; with people, use who.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Marie Curie, who she was born in Warsaw, won two Nobel prizes.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Who is already the subject of the relative clause; repeating she is a calque that doubles the subject.

ejercicios.enunciado: Rewrite the sentence in formal register with preposition + whom.
ejercicios.frase: The lawyer, who I spoke to yesterday, was very helpful.
respuestas: The lawyer, to whom I spoke yesterday, was very helpful.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule preposition + whom/which from Rules and key points applies. In informal register the preposition stays at the end (“who I spoke to”), but in formal register it moves forward and goes before the relative pronoun. After a preposition, the object form whom is used for people: “to whom I spoke”. The preposition is not repeated at the end.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: In formal register the preposition goes before whom.
ejercicios.traduccion: El abogado, con quien hablé ayer, fue muy útil.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The lawyer, to who I spoke yesterday, was very helpful.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After a preposition the object form whom is required, not who.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The lawyer, to whom I spoke to yesterday, was very helpful.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The preposition has been duplicated: if it moves forward before whom, it disappears from the end.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The lawyer, to which I spoke yesterday, was very helpful.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Which is for things; after a preposition, for people, use whom.

ejercicios.enunciado: Join the two sentences with which referring to the whole first clause.
ejercicios.frase: Prices went up again. This annoyed consumers.
respuestas: Prices went up again, which annoyed consumers.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule of which referring to the whole previous clause applies. What annoyed consumers is not “the prices” but the fact that they went up again; that is why the demonstrative this in the second sentence, which sums up the previous idea, is replaced by which. They are joined with a comma: “Prices went up again, which annoyed consumers”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Which picks up the whole idea of the previous clause.
ejercicios.traduccion: Los precios volvieron a subir, lo cual molestó a los consumidores.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Prices went up again, what annoyed consumers.
errores_previstos.explicacion: A calque of Spanish “lo que”: what cannot refer back to a previous clause; use which.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Prices went up again, this annoyed consumers.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Two clauses joined only by a comma (comma splice); you must replace this with which.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Prices went up again, that annoyed consumers.
errores_previstos.explicacion: That is not used after a comma in a non-defining clause and cannot pick up a whole clause.

ejercicios.explicacion: The rule quantifier + of whom / of which applies: the quantifier (none) comes first, then of and finally the relative pronoun. As we are not told what it refers to, the use of which shows that the antecedent is things (for example, “I tried three solutions, none of which worked”). The verb worked closes the relative clause. The order is fixed: quantifier + of + which + verb.

errores_previstos.respuesta: of which none worked
errores_previstos.explicacion: It copies the Spanish order “de las cuales ninguna”; in English the quantifier goes first: none of which.

errores_previstos.respuesta: which none of worked
errores_previstos.explicacion: It separates of from its relative pronoun; the fixed sequence is none of which.

ejercicios.explicacion: The rule preposition + whom in formal register applies: the preposition moves forward and goes before the relative pronoun. Whom, the object form, is the only valid option after a preposition for people. Then comes the relative clause with its subject and verb: “with whom I work” (for example, “my colleagues, with whom I work”). Whom I work with, with the preposition at the end, is also accepted: it is correct, although slightly less formal; what is not accepted is with who.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Preposition + whom in formal register; the preposition at the end is also fine (whom I work with).

errores_previstos.respuesta: I work with whom
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the order of a main clause; in a relative clause the relative pronoun (with its preposition) goes first: with whom I work.

errores_previstos.respuesta: with I whom work
errores_previstos.explicacion: The relative pronoun must come immediately after the preposition: with whom, and then the subject I and the verb.

descripcion_larga_es: Non-defining relative clauses add an extra piece of information about something that is already identified and go between commas. In English they have strict rules: they never allow that, the pronoun cannot be left out, and which can pick up a whole clause (Spanish “lo cual”). Spanish speakers find them difficult because in Spanish “que” works for everything, whereas in English you have to choose between who, whom, which, whose or where.

contexto.que_es: A non-defining relative clause is a subordinate clause that adds information about an antecedent we already know, like an aside. It goes between commas and, if you remove it, the main sentence still makes complete sense. It is introduced by who, whom, which, whose, where or when, never by that.
contexto.por_que_importa: They are very common in written language (the press, reports, biographies) because they allow you to condense two ideas into one sentence. Confusing them with defining clauses changes the meaning: “the students, who were tired, went home” talks about all the students, whereas without commas it talks only about some of them. In a written exam, using that after a comma or leaving out the pronoun are mistakes the examiner spots immediately.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: They are used when the antecedent is a proper noun, something unique or something already identified (my mother, the Prado, Seville) and we want to add a piece of information. Also to comment on a whole previous clause with which (Spanish “lo cual, lo que”). Spanish speakers tend to translate “que” as that in every case and “lo que” as what; in non-defining clauses both options are wrong.
